entries.title: Big Five Personality Traits: The 5-Factor Model of Personality
entries.finding: O describes openness to novelty; C organization and self-discipline; E sociability and talkativeness; A compassion and cooperation; N negative emotional reactivity. Traits are continua, not four-letter types.
entries.label: Evidence
entries.writer_takeaway: Use high/mid/low as drafting contrasts rather than diagnoses or fixed dialogue rules.
entries.limitations: Educational synthesis, not a primary experiment.

entries.title: Personality in its natural habitat: Manifestations and implicit folk theories of personality in daily life
entries.inspected: University of Arizona publication page and abstract
entries.finding: An EAR sampled ambient sounds from 96 people across two days; Big Five scores related to everyday social interaction, moods, activities, and language, and listeners judged extraversion especially well from the audio. Many manifestations were gender-specific.
entries.label: Evidence
entries.writer_takeaway: Make extraversion audible through social initiative and interactive energy, but do not assert an exact words-per-line effect from this abstract.
entries.limitations: Abstract does not report individual word-category coefficients or a universal verbosity threshold; short observation window.

entries.title: Using Linguistic Cues for the Automatic Recognition of Personality in Conversation and Text
entries.inspected: JAIR article landing page and full abstract; PDF link itself was not text-extractable
entries.finding: Big Five prediction from conversational and written linguistic features exceeded baseline for some traits; ranking models performed best overall, observer ratings were easier to model than self-reports, and optimal features varied by trait.
entries.label: Evidence
entries.writer_takeaway: Differentiate several cues together (turn length, social focus, stance) rather than assigning a single signature word.
entries.limitations: Abstract gives no robust trait-specific words or effect sizes; prediction is imperfect and context-sensitive.

entries.title: Linguistic styles: language use as an individual difference
entries.finding: Word-use dimensions showed consistency across multiple writing samples and corresponded modestly with personality measures; linguistic style supplies information beyond story content.
entries.label: Evidence
entries.writer_takeaway: Keep recurring stylistic tendencies across situations, with stress-driven changes rather than a catchphrase per person.
entries.limitations: Written diaries and assignments, not direct dialogue; authors explicitly describe modest effect sizes.

entries.title: The links between bloggers’ personalities and their use of words
entries.inspected: British Psychological Society Research Digest article body
entries.finding: In 694 bloggers, higher neuroticism tracked more negative-emotion words, extraversion more positive-emotion words, agreeableness fewer swear words and more communality words, and conscientiousness more achievement words. Openness associated with more prepositions and formal, longer words rather than the expected intellectual/sensory categories.
entries.label: Evidence
entries.writer_takeaway: Use group/social and positive words for sociable voices; negative appraisal when threatened; allow an agreeable roaster to soften insults.
entries.limitations: Secondary summary of long-form blog writing; correlations do not dictate single lines, and the sample was predominantly female.

entries.title: Bloggers’ reveal personalities with word choice
entries.finding: The university report describes specific-word associations in bloggers; neuroticism accompanied negative adjectives such as terrible/worse, while extraversion accompanied social-outing terms.
entries.label: Evidence
entries.writer_takeaway: Give worried characters occasional negative appraisal, not a rote trait-word checklist; let extroverts frame events as shared experiences.
entries.limitations: University news coverage, not the paper; written blog correlations and particular keywords are poor prescriptions for spoken fiction.

entries.title: Romantic love conceptualized as an attachment process
entries.finding: Two questionnaire studies extended secure, avoidant, and anxious/ambivalent attachment ideas to adult romantic love; groups differed in romantic experience and relationship models.
entries.label: Evidence
entries.writer_takeaway: Treat attachment as a relational stress tendency, not a complete personality or a predetermined outcome.
entries.limitations: Original categorical model and self-report design; not evidence that any one line proves an attachment style.

entries.title: A Brief Overview of Adult Attachment Theory and Research
entries.inspected: Researcher-authored overview, including adult individual differences and anxiety/avoidance sections
entries.finding: Adult attachment is commonly described on anxiety and avoidance dimensions; anxious people may worry they are not fully loved and react when needs go unmet, while avoidant people may downplay dependence. Responsive partners support exploration.
entries.label: Evidence
entries.writer_takeaway: Distinguish Leia’s reassurance check from her agency in choosing; Ryan’s minimization can coexist with real concern.
entries.limitations: Overview synthesizes studies; orientations are dimensions and context-dependent, not diagnoses or gender rules.

entries.title: Conflict in Close Relationships: An Attachment Perspective
entries.finding: In videotaped dating-couple problem discussions, more ambivalent participants evaluated the partner/relationship less positively after a major issue; ambivalent women in this sample showed stronger stress and more negative behavior, while more avoidant men appeared less warm and supportive on major issues.
entries.label: Evidence
entries.writer_takeaway: In the bad route, let Leia seek clarity while Ryan’s visible warmth drops; do not transplant sample-specific gender effects into every scene.
entries.limitations: Abstract only; conditional effects in a particular sample, not proof of exact phrasing.

entries.title: The longitudinal impact of demand and withdrawal during marital conflict
entries.finding: Forty-eight couples completed recorded problem-solving discussions; demandingness and, to a lesser extent, withdrawal correlated with satisfaction, and withdrawal by men plus woman-demand/man-withdraw around woman-identified issues predicted wives’ satisfaction decline over follow-up.
entries.label: Evidence
entries.writer_takeaway: Show the escalating loop rather than treating either person as the sole villain: more questions, then clipped replies and retreat, then further pursuit.
entries.limitations: Observational associations in married couples; this does not establish causation or universal sex roles.

entries.title: The Four Horsemen: Stonewalling
entries.inspected: Gottman Institute article body and suggested antidote
entries.finding: Stonewalling is disengagement during a difficult exchange, often attributed to feeling overwhelmed; the article describes tuning out, turning away, and appearing busy, and recommends a time-out with return to conversation.
entries.label: Evidence
entries.writer_takeaway: Stage Ryan’s “I’m fine” as one avoidant move followed by observable withdrawal; a healthier branch explicitly pauses and comes back.
entries.limitations: Practitioner explanation, not a standalone experimental estimate; a single brief pause is not necessarily stonewalling.

leia.reason: Her affectionate play and excited run-on turns suggest high social energy and warmth, while curiosity about new experiences supports high O (P01, P02). Checking Ryan’s face after a bold choice and fearing judgment suggests attachment anxiety under uncertainty (P07, P08), but her explicit choices and willingness to explore rule out treating her as passive. In a bad-route conflict, reassurance bids can intensify if Ryan withdraws (P09, P10); this is a fiction-writing inference, not a diagnosis.
predicted_habits: Give her longer, linked turns when excited; she circles back to add one more thought rather than always speaking in fragments (P01, P02; inference).
Favor affectionate we/us and shared-experience language over sharp insults; her teasing lands warmly (P05; extrapolated to speech).
After a bold flirtation or consensual new choice, insert a brief direct check of Ryan’s reaction, not a request for permission (P08; inference).
When she senses distance, move from a joking probe to a plain “Are we okay?” rather than repetitive pleading (P08, P09; inference).

ryan.attachment: avoidant-leaning under conflict; otherwise capable of security
ryan.reason: His decent, unshowy manner and plain narration suggest high A and lower outward E, not a global lack of social skill (P01, P02). Fear of seeming boring or jealous adds situational negative reactivity, while guilt makes him over-explain. His “I’m fine” followed by disengagement is a plausible avoidant-leaning stress move (P08, P09); repeated demand-withdraw can damage the relationship (P10, P11). This describes a route-specific behavior, not a clinical classification.
predicted_habits: Use plain concrete clauses and dry self-directed jokes; keep his ordinary turns shorter than Leia’s and Julian’s (P01, P02; stylistic inference).
When jealous, shorten responses and omit the actual feeling; do not claim that the phrase “I’m fine” is itself a validated marker (P08, P11).
When caught in a mistake, switch to overly precise, chained explanations and qualifiers (character-note inference; P04 cautions that style is not deterministic).
In the healthy route, name the need for a break and explicitly return to the conversation instead of silently disappearing (P11).

julian.reason: Hosting, booming presence, and theatrical rambling put him high on outward E (P01, P02); loyal warmth and a craving to be liked coexist with a mid A profile because his bluster can crowd others out. Panic may temporarily increase his talk rather than prove a stable trait, so N stays mid (P03, P04). Secure-leaning is a provisional narrative choice: loneliness and wanting approval are not enough to infer anxious attachment without persistent fear of abandonment (P07, P08).
predicted_habits: Let him own the longest turns: elaborate setup, comic detour, and extravagant conclusion (P01, P02; inference, not a measured word count).
Use socially inclusive invitations, praise, and shared-party framing when hosting (P05; extrapolated from writing).
When scared or awkward, talk more and escalate absurd specificity, then offer a sincere repair when someone is hurt (character-note inference).
Occasionally end a boast with a quick, quiet check that people are actually enjoying themselves (P08; narrative inference).

maya.reason: Her quick questions, interruption, hype, and willingness to engage new people imply high E and O (P01, P02). She notices harm and drops the bit to support someone, which makes A high despite bluntness and roast humor; agreeableness does not require never teasing (P05). Her steadiness in emotionally difficult moments supports a secure-leaning writing choice, though attachment cannot be established from the notes alone (P07, P08).
predicted_habits: Write fast turn-taking with interruptions, pointed questions, and short-to-medium bursts, contrasting Julian’s long monologues (P02, P03; narrative inference).
In group scenes, amplify other people with direct positive and communal language; keep roasts affectionate rather than sustained contempt (P05; extrapolated).
When she sees someone hurting, drop the joke and ask one specific, unembellished question (P08; narrative inference).
Around Julian, use teasing as a conversational cover for attention, then briefly become direct when stakes rise (character-note inference).
